item.title: More than 30 Dakuinuku families relocate as high tidal waves threaten homes
item.description: More than 30 families in Dakuinuku Village, Tailevu, have relocated to another part of the village as coastal erosion and waves during high tide continue to threaten their homes. Turaga ni Koro, Iokimi Dau says the families have moved to land identified by their yavusa because of concerns about waves entering parts of the village.
item.content:encoded:
More than 30 families in Dakuinuku Village, Tailevu, have relocated to another part of the village as coastal erosion and waves during high tide continue to threaten their homes.

Turaga ni Koro, Iokimi Dau says the families have moved to land identified by their yavusa because of concerns about waves entering parts of the village.

Dau, who is in his fourth year as Turaga ni Koro, says the situation has become a major concern for villagers, with families fearing they may have to relocate again if the problem is not addressed.

Insert:Dau on families relocating (VITIFM). 15th October,26

He believes changing climate conditions and problems with the seawall built to protect the village have made the situation worse.

Dau says the seawall was not properly completed and says waves continue to enter parts of the village during high tide.

He says the seawall project was carried out by the company in question before he became Turaga ni Koro and says the company has not returned to undertake further work.

Dau is calling on the company and the relevant authorities to inspect the seawall and undertake the necessary work to better protect the village.

He says villagers want a long-term solution to the problem so families can feel safe in their homes and avoid having to relocate again.

item.title: Fiji must address inequality, drugs and HIV alongside immunity debate – Tui Nayau
item.description: Fiji cannot achieve lasting reconciliation by addressing immunity alone while economic inequality, drug-related problems and HIV continue to affect communities across the country. Tui Nayau Ratu Tevita Lutunauga Kapaiwai Uluilakeba Mara says reconciliation requires more than changes to the law, and must also address the social and economic challenges facing Fijians.
item.content:encoded:
Fiji cannot achieve lasting reconciliation by addressing immunity alone while economic inequality, drug-related problems and HIV continue to affect communities across the country.

Tui Nayau Ratu Tevita Lutunauga Kapaiwai Uluilakeba Mara says reconciliation requires more than changes to the law, and must also address the social and economic challenges facing Fijians.

Speaking on the public consultations on the Constitution Amendment Bill, Ratu Tevita says he respects the Supreme Court's opinion on immunity, but believes the country must also confront the deeper issues that have contributed to social tensions.

He says many iTaukei families are still struggling to benefit from Fiji's economy, 56 years after the country gained independence.

Ratu Tevita says these economic concerns were among the issues exploited during the political upheavals of 1987 and 2000.

He stresses that taking power by force can never be justified, but says the underlying problems that were exploited during those periods must also be addressed if Fiji is to achieve lasting reconciliation.

Ratu Tevita also raised concerns about the impact of drugs and HIV on young people and communities, saying the vanua, churches, families and Government must work together to address these challenges.

He says national unity also requires respect, understanding and responsible leadership.

The Tui Nayau condemned threatening social media comments directed at people who criticised chiefs, saying Fiji's traditional leaders do not need to be defended through threats or intimidation.

He says while people should respect Fiji's chiefs and traditional institutions, criticism and disrespect should be answered with dignity rather than threats.

Ratu Tevita also stressed that Indo-Fijians, descendants of the girmitiya and every community that calls Fiji home belong to the country.

He welcomed recent comments by RFMF Commander Major General Ro Jone Kalouniwai that the people's vote must be protected and respected.

Ratu Tevita says Fiji now needs leaders at every level to use words that bring people together, address the challenges facing communities and find a common path towards national unity.

item.title: Defence challenges admissibility of DNA report in RFMF armoury break-in case
item.description: The defence is challenging the admissibility of a DNA report in the case of Isaia Ledua, who is alleged to have attempted to break into the Republic of Fiji Military Forces armoury at Queen Elizabeth Barracks in Nabua in April this year. State lawyer Hezekiah Nofaga informed the court that the prosecution had submitted the proposed agreed facts, but had yet to receive a response from the defence.
item.content:encoded:
The defence is challenging the admissibility of a DNA report in the case of Isaia Ledua, who is alleged to have attempted to break into the Republic of Fiji Military Forces armoury at Queen Elizabeth Barracks in Nabua in April this year. State lawyer Hezekiah Nofaga informed the court that the prosecution had submitted the proposed agreed facts, but had yet to receive a response from the defence. Ledua's lawyer, Jerry Dinati did not appear in court as he is in Labasa. Ledua is charged with one count of aggravated burglary and one count of damaging property.

It is alleged that between 8th and 9th April, Ledua attempted to break into the RFMF Ammunition Magazine building in Nabua and damaged the door lock keypad during the same period.

item.title: FRCS clarifies yacht clearance procedures and passport issue following Australian visitor’s complaint
item.description: Nilufa Buksh , Navitalai Naivalurua · 15/10/2026 The Fiji Revenue and Customs Service says the captain of a yacht carrying a three-person crew voluntarily informed them in writing that an Australian visitor would not be travelling to the vessel's next overseas port of call.
item.content:encoded:
Nilufa Buksh , Navitalai Naivalurua · 15/10/2026

The Fiji Revenue and Customs Service says the captain of a yacht carrying a three-person crew voluntarily informed them in writing that an Australian visitor would not be travelling to the vessel's next overseas port of call.

FRCS says this declaration was taken into account when processing the yacht's outward clearance following a complaint by the Australian visitor over an alleged cash payment demand and the retention of his passport at Denarau Marina.

It says under section 72(1) of the Customs Act 1986, a vessel’s master must obtain clearance before departing Fiji for an overseas destination.

FRCS says section 72(2)(b) and (c) require the master, owner or authorised agent to answer questions about the vessel, crew, passengers and voyage, and provide the required vessel and passenger documentation.

FRCS says the departure documentation therefore needed to accurately reflect who would be travelling aboard the yacht.

It confirms that the captain initially held the visitor's passport and says it subsequently liaised with Immigration, after which the passport was returned to the captain.

FRCS also confirms that it did not detain the visitor.

It says it understands that the visitor holds a valid outbound ticket and is expected to leave Fiji by the end of October 2026.

FRCS says it remains committed to fulfilling its border protection responsibilities under the Customs Act and treating all visitors to Fiji’s ports with courtesy, respect and in accordance with the law.

This follows a formal complaint lodged by an Australian visitor with FRCS, alleging that a Customs Officer at Denarau Marina demanded a FJ$240 cash payment, refused his offer to pay part of the amount by EFTPOS and retained his passport.

The visitor claims the officer insisted that he withdraw additional cash from an ATM after saying the EFTPOS machine was not working.

He also alleges that the officer told him he would not be allowed to leave Fiji unless he paid the amount.

The visitor has raised concerns about the legal basis for the charge, payment procedures, the retention of his passport and questions about whether he would continue on the voyage.

He says the incident led to the yacht's captain deciding to disembark him from the vessel.

item.title: Serevi considers entering politics ahead of next general elections
item.description: Speaking on fijivillage Straight Talk with Vijay Narayan, Serevi says he is thinking about doing something new to help Fiji move forward. Insert: Serevi joining Politics 14th Oct 26Â
item.content:encoded:
Speaking on fijivillage Straight Talk with Vijay Narayan, Serevi says he is thinking about doing something new to help Fiji move forward.

Insert: Serevi joining Politics 14th Oct 26Â

He says there are many youth who need guidance and opportunities, and he would be willing to enter politics if given the chance to make a difference.

When asked which political party he is planning to join, Serevi says he is still weighing his options.

He mentioned Unity Fiji among the parties he has been looking at but stressed that no political party has attracted him enough to make a decision.

Serevi says some parties have approached him for meetings, and he is looking forward to having discussions with them.

He says he remains open to speaking with different political parties before deciding on his next move.

Meanwhile, Serevi says his main concern is the future of Fiji's young people, particularly with the growing problems of drugs and HIV in the country.

He says this was one of the main reasons he returned to Fiji after spending many years overseas.

Serevi says he has been back in the country for about 18 months and has already spoken to around 35,000 to 40,000 young people through schools, churches, villages and rugby clubs.

He says his programmes focus on motivating young people, encouraging them to stay away from drugs and helping them set goals for their future.

Through the Serevi International Academy of Rugby, he is also working with boys and girls aged 15 to 18, using rugby to develop their skills and help them become better people.

Serevi believes everyone has a responsibility to help address the challenges facing young people, including parents, community leaders, sportspeople and those in government.

Serevi warns that if people do not work together to address these problems, the situation could become worse in the next five to ten years.

He also believes Fiji needs more unity, saying people should focus on helping one another and building the country rather than bringing others down, particularly on social media.
